direct_claims: This chart is a scatter plot comparing greenhouse gas emissions against the cost to animal welfare across 91 pig production systems in the United Kingdom and Brazil.
Published by Our World in Data, it is based on a 2024 study by Harriet Bartlett et al. titled 'Trade-offs in the externalities of pig production are not inevitable'.
The X-axis represents 'welfare cost,' a metric calculated by weighting the quantity of years lived by quality-of-life scores from detailed welfare assessments.
A positive welfare cost indicates a net negative impact on animal welfare, while a negative value indicates a net benefit to welfare.
The systems are categorized by their finishing system type, such as Slatted, Solid floor, Straw yard, and Outdoor.
derived_claims: The Y-axis measures greenhouse gas emissions in kilograms per kilogram of deadweight, representing the carbon footprint of pork production.

Looking at the distribution, outdoor and straw yard systems tend to cluster on the left side of the chart, indicating lower welfare costs (better welfare), but they exhibit a wider spread of emissions, sometimes reaching much higher levels.
Conversely, slatted floor systems cluster tightly on the right side, indicating higher welfare costs (worse welfare) but generally lower and more consistent greenhouse gas emissions.

However, because the data points overlap significantly—with some systems achieving both low emissions and low welfare costs—the study suggests that these trade-offs are not inevitable, and optimized management practices could potentially achieve both environmental and ethical goals simultaneously.
The highest emission outlier in the dataset is an outdoor/straw yard system emitting over 12 kg of CO2-equivalent per kilogram of deadweight, while maintaining a relatively low welfare cost.
speculative_claims: The visualization aims to explore whether farms must choose between environmental efficiency and ethical animal treatment.

This data illustrates a classic policy dilemma in sustainable agriculture: the tension between intensive farming, which often minimizes greenhouse gas emissions through space and feed efficiency, and extensive farming, which prioritizes animal welfare but may require more resources and generate higher emissions per kilogram of meat.
